Appendix A Weighted-SFT Induced-Target Details

Weighted SFT methods can look identical at the optimizer level because they all minimize a weighted log likelihood. The policy being fit, however, is fixed before optimization begins. The sampler supplies support, the weights assign mass on that support, and the product determines the induced target. Expanding this algebra gives the main-text comparisons a policy-level interpretation: BOLT is compared by the sampler–weight product it induces, not by the shared fact that it uses a supervised fine-tuning optimizer. The same distinction explains why raw-reward weighting can use the same reference rollout set while fitting a different target policy.

Proof of Proposition 1.

Use w⁡(x,y)=w¯​(x)​π~w​(y∣x)/q⁡(y∣x)w(x,y)=\bar{w}(x)\tilde{\pi}_{w}(y\mid x)/q(y\mid x) and substitute into the weighted negative log-likelihood. The conditional loss becomes w¯​(x)​𝔼π~w​[−log⁡πθ​(y∣x)]\bar{w}(x)\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{\pi}_{w}}\left[-\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right], which is w¯(x)[DKL(π~w∥πθ)+H(π~w)]\bar{w}(x)[D_{\text{KL}}(\tilde{\pi}_{w}\|\pi_{\theta})+H(\tilde{\pi}_{w})]. ∎

Proof of Theorem 4.

If π~w=π∗\tilde{\pi}_{w}=\pi^{*}, then every set with zero qq-mass also has zero π~w\tilde{\pi}_{w}-mass and therefore zero π∗\pi^{*}-mass, giving π∗≪q\pi^{*}\ll q. On the support of qq,

q⁡(y∣x)​w​(x,y)w¯​(x)=π∗​(y∣x),\frac{q(y\mid x)w(x,y)}{\bar{w}(x)}=\pi^{*}(y\mid x), (29)

which gives the displayed density-ratio identity. Conversely, substituting that identity into q⁡(y∣x)​w​(x,y)/w¯​(x)q(y\mid x)w(x,y)/\bar{w}(x) gives π∗​(y∣x)\pi^{*}(y\mid x). The reference-sampled specialization q=πrefq=\pi_{\text{ref}} cancels the reference-policy ratio and gives the BOLT weight up to prompt scale. ∎

Proof of Corollary 5.

Apply the reverse-KL value identity (30) with π=π~w\pi=\tilde{\pi}_{w}. ∎

The algebra gives a direct way to read the baselines in the experiments. For BOLT, q≜πrefq\triangleq\pi_{\text{ref}}, w⁡(x,y)≜exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/β)/Z⁡(x)w(x,y)\triangleq\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)/Z(x), w¯​(x)=1\bar{w}(x)=1, and π~w=π∗\tilde{\pi}_{w}=\pi^{*} exactly. A Refit-style baseline can hold the sampler fixed at q=πrefq=\pi_{\text{ref}} but use raw reward weights w⁡(x,y)≜r⁡(x,y)w(x,y)\triangleq r(x,y); the original Refit objective is written for a logged behavior policy π0\pi_{0}. In either case, raw reward weighting induces a reward-weighted logged distribution rather than the Boltzmann target policy. Demonstration-based methods fit an implicit target determined by curated samples, so their mismatch with fixed-reference RLVR is governed by both the available curated support and the distance between the curated target and the KL-regularized Boltzmann target policy.

Appendix B Boltzmann Projection Proofs

The projection chain has one role: it identifies the policy targeted by a faithful static weighted-SFT objective. The fixed-reference reward–KL objective selects the Boltzmann target policy; the forward projection onto that target becomes weighted maximum likelihood under reference rollouts; and the induced-target condition forces the Boltzmann density-ratio weight. The support condition remains explicit throughout the proofs because it is the first place where reference-policy coverage enters the algorithm: if πref\pi_{\text{ref}} assigns zero mass to a completion, neither the Boltzmann target nor a reference-sampled estimator can recover it.

Proof of Proposition 2.

Fix xx and write μ≜πref(⋅∣x)\mu\triangleq\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x). Any feasible policy π(⋅∣x)≪μ\pi(\cdot\mid x)\ll\mu has density f=d​π/d​μf=d\pi/d\mu. Let Z⁡(x)=∫exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/β)​𝑑μ​(y)Z(x)=\int\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)\,d\mu(y) and define f∗​(y)=exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/β)/Z⁡(x)f^{*}(y)=\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)/Z(x). Since rr is bounded, Z⁡(x)Z(x) is finite and positive. The prompt-wise objective can be rewritten as

∫f⁡(y)​r​(x,y)​𝑑μ​(y)−β​∫f⁡(y)​log⁡f⁡(y)​𝑑μ​(y)=β​log⁡Z⁡(x)−β​∫f⁡(y)​log​f⁡(y)f∗​(y)​𝑑μ​(y).\int f(y)r(x,y)\,d\mu(y)-\beta\int f(y)\log f(y)\,d\mu(y)=\beta\log Z(x)-\beta\int f(y)\log\frac{f(y)}{f^{*}(y)}\,d\mu(y).

The final term is βDKL(π∥π∗)\beta D_{\text{KL}}(\pi\|\pi^{*}), so the objective is maximized uniquely at f=f∗f=f^{*} almost surely. The same display gives, after averaging over prompts, the reverse-KL value identity

𝒥RL(π∗)−𝒥RL(π)=β𝔼x[DKL(π(⋅∣x)∥π∗(⋅∣x))].\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi^{*})-\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi)=\beta\,\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[D_{\text{KL}}\!\left(\pi(\cdot\mid x)\,\middle\|\,\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)\right)\right]. (30)

∎

Proof of Theorem 3.

With q=πrefq=\pi_{\text{ref}} and w⁡(x,y)=exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/β)/Z⁡(x)w(x,y)=\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)/Z(x), w¯​(x)=𝔼πref​[w⁡(x,y)]=1\bar{w}(x)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}}[w(x,y)]=1. Proposition 1 therefore gives

π~w​(y∣x)=πref​(y∣x)​exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/β)Z⁡(x)=π∗​(y∣x).\tilde{\pi}_{w}(y\mid x)=\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\frac{\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)}{Z(x)}=\pi^{*}(y\mid x). (31)

For fixed xx,

DKL(π∗∥πθ)=−H(π∗)−𝔼y∼π∗(⋅∣x)[logπθ(y∣x)].D_{\text{KL}}(\pi^{*}\|\pi_{\theta})=-H(\pi^{*})-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right]. (32)

The entropy term does not depend on θ\theta. Converting the expectation under π∗\pi^{*} to one under πref\pi_{\text{ref}} using (4) gives

𝔼y∼π∗​[log⁡πθ​(y∣x)]=𝔼y∼πref​[exp⁡(r⁡(x,y)/β)Z⁡(x)​log⁡πθ​(y∣x)].\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi^{*}}\left[\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi_{\text{ref}}}\left[\frac{\exp(r(x,y)/\beta)}{Z(x)}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right]. (33)

Negating gives the weighted maximum-likelihood objective. ∎

The preceding proof fixes the target policy. The remaining population question is whether fitting that target by forward KL also certifies the reverse-KL value used by RLVR. In a realizable model class, the direction difference disappears because both divergences reach zero at π∗\pi^{*}. Outside realizability, the paper needs a local transfer condition rather than a global equivalence claim. Corollary 15 states the clean boundary, and Appendix C gives the local comparison used by the finite one-shot theorem.

Corollary 15 (Realizability).

Let Θ\Theta be the model class and define F(θ)≜𝔼x[DKL(π∗(⋅∣x)∥πθ(⋅∣x))]F(\theta)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{x}[D_{\text{KL}}(\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x))]. If π∗(⋅∣x)∈{πθ(⋅∣x):θ∈Θ}\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)\in\{\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x):\theta\in\Theta\} for almost every xx, then every global minimizer of FF satisfies πθ=π∗\pi_{\theta}=\pi^{*} almost surely and therefore maximizes 𝒥RL\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}.

Proof of Corollary 15.

The forward KL is nonnegative and equals zero if and only if πθ(⋅∣x)=π∗(⋅∣x)\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)=\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x) almost surely. If π∗\pi^{*} is in the model class, the global minimum of FF is zero. The reverse-KL identity in (30) then shows that the same policy maximizes the original KL-regularized RLVR objective. ∎

Appendix C Local Forward/Reverse-KL Comparability

Outside realizability, target matching and value certification become separate questions. Weighted likelihood fits the Boltzmann target by forward KL, whereas the fixed-reference RLVR value gap is reverse KL to the same target. Nearby distributions have the same second-order information-geometric geometry [1], but that local fact is useful only when the fitted policy remains in a controlled density-ratio neighborhood of π∗\pi^{*}. The boundary is exact: the local comparison supports value transfer for a fitted policy, while a stronger two-sided condition is needed before comparing the forward and reverse population projections under misspecification.

Proposition 16 (Local Forward/Reverse KL Comparison).

For any prompt, let P≜π∗(⋅∣x)P\triangleq\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x) and Q≜πθ(⋅∣x)Q\triangleq\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x). Define u⁡(y)≜P⁡(y)/Q⁡(y)−1u(y)\triangleq P(y)/Q(y)-1 and assume ρ≜supy|u⁡(y)|<1\rho\triangleq\sup_{y}|u(y)|<1. Then

DKL(P∥Q)\displaystyle D_{\text{KL}}(P\|Q) =12χ2(P∥Q)+Rf,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\chi^{2}(P\|Q)+R_{f}, DKL(Q∥P)\displaystyle D_{\text{KL}}(Q\|P) =12χ2(P∥Q)+Rr,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\chi^{2}(P\|Q)+R_{r}, (34)
|Rf|\displaystyle|R_{f}| ≤ρ3​(1−ρ)212χ2(P∥Q),\displaystyle\leq\frac{\rho}{3(1-\rho)^{2}}\frac{1}{2}\chi^{2}(P\|Q), |Rr|\displaystyle|R_{r}| ≤2​ρ3​(1−ρ)312χ2(P∥Q).\displaystyle\leq\frac{2\rho}{3(1-\rho)^{3}}\frac{1}{2}\chi^{2}(P\|Q).

Here χ2(P∥Q)≜∑yQ(y)(P(y)/Q(y)−1)2\chi^{2}(P\|Q)\triangleq\sum_{y}Q(y)(P(y)/Q(y)-1)^{2}.

Proof of Proposition 16.

Write P⁡(y)=Q⁡(y)​(1+u⁡(y))P(y)=Q(y)(1+u(y)) with ∑yQ⁡(y)​u​(y)=0\sum_{y}Q(y)u(y)=0. For the forward KL,

DKL(P∥Q)=∑yQ(y)(1+u(y))log(1+u(y)).D_{\text{KL}}(P\|Q)=\sum_{y}Q(y)(1+u(y))\log(1+u(y)). (35)

The Taylor expansion (1+u)​log⁡(1+u)=u+12​u2+hf​(u)(1+u)\log(1+u)=u+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}+h_{f}(u) has hf′′′​(u)=−(1+u)−2h_{f}^{\prime\prime\prime}(u)=-(1+u)^{-2}, so |hf​(u)|≤|u|3/(6​(1−ρ)2)|h_{f}(u)|\leq|u|^{3}/(6(1-\rho)^{2}). This yields the stated RfR_{f} bound. For reverse KL, −log⁡(1+u)=−u+12​u2+hr​(u)-\log(1+u)=-u+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}+h_{r}(u) with hr′′′​(u)=−2​(1+u)−3h_{r}^{\prime\prime\prime}(u)=-2(1+u)^{-3}, giving |hr​(u)|≤|u|3/(3​(1−ρ)3)|h_{r}(u)|\leq|u|^{3}/(3(1-\rho)^{3}) and the stated RrR_{r} bound. ∎

Proposition 16 is deliberately local. It shows that, when the fitted policy is already close to π∗\pi^{*} in density ratio, forward and reverse KL have comparable quadratic cores and controlled remainders. The one-sided value certificate applies this comparison to one fitted policy. It does not claim that minimizing forward KL over a misspecified class always gives the same projection as minimizing reverse KL; that stronger statement needs both candidate projections to remain in the same local regime.

Proposition 17 (One-Sided Value Transfer for a Fitted Policy).

Let R(θ)≜𝔼x[DKL(πθ(⋅∣x)∥π∗(⋅∣x))]R(\theta)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{x}[D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\|\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x))] and F(θ)≜𝔼x[DKL(π∗(⋅∣x)∥πθ(⋅∣x))]F(\theta)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{x}[D_{\text{KL}}(\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)\|\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x))]. If a fitted policy θ\theta satisfies supy|π∗​(y∣x)/πθ​(y∣x)−1|≤ρ<1\sup_{y}|\pi^{*}(y\mid x)/\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)-1|\leq\rho<1 almost surely, and aρ≜ρ/(3​(1−ρ)2)<1a_{\rho}\triangleq\rho/(3(1-\rho)^{2})<1, then

R⁡(θ)≤κρ​F​(θ),κρ≜1+2​ρ/(3​(1−ρ)3)1−aρ.R(\theta)\leq\kappa_{\rho}F(\theta),\qquad\kappa_{\rho}\triangleq\frac{1+2\rho/(3(1-\rho)^{3})}{1-a_{\rho}}. (36)

Consequently 𝒥RL​(π∗)−𝒥RL​(πθ)≤β​κρ​F​(θ)\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi^{*})-\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi_{\theta})\leq\beta\kappa_{\rho}F(\theta). A sufficient log-ratio trust-region condition is supy|log⁡(πθ​(y∣x)/π∗​(y∣x))|≤B<log⁡2\sup_{y}|\log(\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)/\pi^{*}(y\mid x))|\leq B<\log 2, with ρ=eB−1\rho=e^{B}-1.

Proof of Proposition 17.

For each prompt, Proposition 16 gives

DKL(P∥Q)≥(1−aρ)12χ2(P∥Q),DKL(Q∥P)≤(1+bρ)12χ2(P∥Q),D_{\text{KL}}(P\|Q)\geq(1-a_{\rho})\frac{1}{2}\chi^{2}(P\|Q),\qquad D_{\text{KL}}(Q\|P)\leq(1+b_{\rho})\frac{1}{2}\chi^{2}(P\|Q),

where aρ≜ρ/(3​(1−ρ)2)a_{\rho}\triangleq\rho/(3(1-\rho)^{2}) and bρ≜2​ρ/(3​(1−ρ)3)b_{\rho}\triangleq 2\rho/(3(1-\rho)^{3}). Averaging over prompts yields R⁡(θ)≤((1+bρ)/(1−aρ))​F​(θ)R(\theta)\leq((1+b_{\rho})/(1-a_{\rho}))F(\theta). The value statement follows from (30). If |log⁡(πθ​(y∣x)/π∗​(y∣x))|≤B|\log(\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)/\pi^{*}(y\mid x))|\leq B, then |u⁡(y)|=|π∗​(y∣x)/πθ​(y∣x)−1|≤eB−1|u(y)|=|\pi^{*}(y\mid x)/\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)-1|\leq e^{B}-1. Thus B<log⁡2B<\log 2 implies ρ=eB−1<1\rho=e^{B}-1<1. ∎

For the Boltzmann target, the local condition has a concrete temperature reading. Since log⁡(π∗​(y∣x)/πref​(y∣x))=r⁡(x,y)/β−log⁡Z⁡(x)\log(\pi^{*}(y\mid x)/\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x))=r(x,y)/\beta-\log Z(x) and log⁡Z⁡(x)∈[rmin/β,rmax/β]\log Z(x)\in[r_{\min}/\beta,r_{\max}/\beta], the target is a bounded multiplicative tilt of the reference policy: supy|log⁡(π∗​(y∣x)/πref​(y∣x))|≤Δ​r/β\sup_{y}|\log(\pi^{*}(y\mid x)/\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x))|\leq\Delta r/\beta, where Δ​r≜rmax−rmin\Delta r\triangleq r_{\max}-r_{\min}. If a fitted policy also stays within a sup-log-density radius τ\tau of the reference policy, then supy|log⁡(π∗​(y∣x)/πθ​(y∣x))|≤Δ​r/β+τ\sup_{y}|\log(\pi^{*}(y\mid x)/\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x))|\leq\Delta r/\beta+\tau. The assumption ρ<1\rho<1 is therefore implied by the explicit local regime Δ​r/β+τ<log⁡2\Delta r/\beta+\tau<\log 2. This is intentionally a local statement: small temperatures or large reward ranges can leave this regime before optimization begins, which is why the main one-shot theorem pays an explicit forward approximation term rather than claiming global forward/reverse projection equivalence.

Remark. A rare-action example shows why the local condition is necessary. On two actions, let Pϵ=(ϵ,1−ϵ)P_{\epsilon}=(\epsilon,1-\epsilon) and Qϵ=(δϵ,1−δϵ)Q_{\epsilon}=(\delta_{\epsilon},1-\delta_{\epsilon}) with δϵ↓0\delta_{\epsilon}\downarrow 0 and ϵ=exp(−1/δϵ2)\epsilon=\exp(-1/\delta_{\epsilon}^{2}). Then DKL(Pϵ∥Qϵ)→0D_{\text{KL}}(P_{\epsilon}\|Q_{\epsilon})\to 0, but DKL(Qϵ∥Pϵ)→∞D_{\text{KL}}(Q_{\epsilon}\|P_{\epsilon})\to\infty. Thus a small forward KL can still place too much mass on a target-rare action, which is exactly the failure mode that reverse-KL RLVR value penalizes.

The one-sided certificate is enough for Theorem 9, which evaluates the learned policy after fitting. A projection-level comparison asks for more: if the forward and reverse KL minimizers over a misspecified class are both local to the Boltzmann target, then their values are comparable. Corollary 18 keeps this stronger claim separate from the main text so that the misspecified case is not overstated.

Corollary 18 (Local Projection Transfer under Misspecification).

Choose population projections θF∈arg​minθ∈Θ⁡F​(θ)\theta_{\text{F}}\in\argmin_{\theta\in\Theta}F(\theta) and θR∈arg​minθ∈Θ⁡R​(θ)\theta_{\text{R}}\in\argmin_{\theta\in\Theta}R(\theta). Suppose that both projections satisfy, almost surely with a common ρ<1\rho<1, supy|π∗​(y∣x)/πθ​(y∣x)−1|≤ρ\sup_{y}|\pi^{*}(y\mid x)/\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)-1|\leq\rho for θ∈{θF,θR}\theta\in\{\theta_{\text{F}},\theta_{\text{R}}\}. Set aρ≜ρ/(3​(1−ρ)2)a_{\rho}\triangleq\rho/(3(1-\rho)^{2}) and bρ≜2​ρ/(3​(1−ρ)3)b_{\rho}\triangleq 2\rho/(3(1-\rho)^{3}), assume aρ<1a_{\rho}<1 and bρ<1b_{\rho}<1, and define Γρ≜(1+bρ)​(1+aρ)/[(1−aρ)​(1−bρ)]\Gamma_{\rho}\triangleq(1+b_{\rho})(1+a_{\rho})/[(1-a_{\rho})(1-b_{\rho})]. Then

R⁡(θF)≤Γρ​R​(θR),𝒥RL​(πθR)−𝒥RL​(πθF)≤β⁡(Γρ−1)​R​(θR).R(\theta_{\text{F}})\leq\Gamma_{\rho}R(\theta_{\text{R}}),\qquad\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi_{\theta_{\text{R}}})-\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi_{\theta_{\text{F}}})\leq\beta(\Gamma_{\rho}-1)R(\theta_{\text{R}}). (37)
Proof of Corollary 18.

For a fixed θ\theta, write

C(θ)≜𝔼x[χ2(π∗(⋅∣x)∥πθ(⋅∣x))/2].C(\theta)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[\chi^{2}\!\left(\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\right)/2\right].

(1−aρ)​C​(θ)≤F⁡(θ)≤(1+aρ)​C​(θ)(1-a_{\rho})C(\theta)\leq F(\theta)\leq(1+a_{\rho})C(\theta)

and

(1−bρ)​C​(θ)≤R⁡(θ)≤(1+bρ)​C​(θ),bρ≜2​ρ3​(1−ρ)3.(1-b_{\rho})C(\theta)\leq R(\theta)\leq(1+b_{\rho})C(\theta),\qquad b_{\rho}\triangleq\frac{2\rho}{3(1-\rho)^{3}}.

The lower bounds use aρ<1a_{\rho}<1 and bρ<1b_{\rho}<1. Applying the upper transfer to θF\theta_{\text{F}}, the optimality of θF\theta_{\text{F}} for FF, and then the lower transfer for θR\theta_{\text{R}} gives

R⁡(θF)\displaystyle R(\theta_{\text{F}}) ≤1+bρ1−aρ​F​(θF)≤1+bρ1−aρ​F​(θR)\displaystyle\leq\frac{1+b_{\rho}}{1-a_{\rho}}F(\theta_{\text{F}})\leq\frac{1+b_{\rho}}{1-a_{\rho}}F(\theta_{\text{R}})
≤(1+bρ)​(1+aρ)(1−aρ)​(1−bρ)​R​(θR)=Γρ​R​(θR).\displaystyle\leq\frac{(1+b_{\rho})(1+a_{\rho})}{(1-a_{\rho})(1-b_{\rho})}R(\theta_{\text{R}})=\Gamma_{\rho}R(\theta_{\text{R}}).

Finally, by (30),

𝒥RL​(πθR)−𝒥RL​(πθF)=β⁡(R⁡(θF)−R⁡(θR))≤β⁡(Γρ−1)​R​(θR),\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi_{\theta_{\text{R}}})-\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi_{\theta_{\text{F}}})=\beta\left(R(\theta_{\text{F}})-R(\theta_{\text{R}})\right)\leq\beta(\Gamma_{\rho}-1)R(\theta_{\text{R}}),

which proves the stated value-excess bound. ∎

Appendix D Reference Coverage and Normalizer Estimation

Coverage and normalizer estimation both arise during rollout generation, but they answer different questions. Coverage asks whether useful completions appear in the stored set at all. Normalizer estimation asks whether the weights on already observed completions are rescaled accurately. The distinction matters because missing support is not a concentration error: a sharply estimated normalizer on all-negative rollouts still leaves the target mass outside the dataset. The estimator components therefore separate support, self-normalized rescaling, and prompt allocation before they are combined in the one-shot certificate.

The first estimator component treats the oracle density ratio w=d​π∗/d​πrefw=d\pi^{*}/d\pi_{\text{ref}} as known. Its variance is governed by the second moment of that ratio, so the same weight that matches the RLVR target can reduce the effective sample size when the target is far from the reference policy.

Proposition 19 (ESS-Controlled Estimation Component).

Fix a prompt xx. Let y1,…,yN∼i.i.d.πref(⋅∣x)y_{1},\ldots,y_{N}\overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x), w(x,y)=dπ∗(⋅∣x)/dπref(⋅∣x)w(x,y)=d\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)/d\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x), 𝒞2​(x)≜𝔼πref​[w​(x,y)2]\mathcal{C}_{2}(x)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}}[w(x,y)^{2}], and wmax​(x)≜supyw⁡(x,y)w_{\max}(x)\triangleq\sup_{y}w(x,y). For any loss 0≤ℓ⁡(y)≤L0\leq\ell(y)\leq L, define μ≜𝔼π∗​[ℓ​(y)]\mu\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{\pi^{*}}[\ell(y)] and μ^N≜N−1​∑n=1Nw⁡(x,yn)​ℓ​(yn)\hat{\mu}_{N}\triangleq N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{N}w(x,y_{n})\ell(y_{n}). Then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

|μ^N−μ|≤L​2​𝒞2​(x)​log⁡(2/δ)N+2​L​wmax​(x)​log⁡(2/δ)3​N.|\hat{\mu}_{N}-\mu|\leq L\sqrt{\frac{2\mathcal{C}_{2}(x)\log(2/\delta)}{N}}+\frac{2Lw_{\max}(x)\log(2/\delta)}{3N}. (38)
Corollary 20 (Self-Normalized Prompt Perturbation).

Under Proposition 19, let μ^Nsn≜∑n=1Nw⁡(x,yn)​ℓ​(yn)/∑n=1Nw⁡(x,yn)\hat{\mu}_{N}^{\text{sn}}\triangleq\sum_{n=1}^{N}w(x,y_{n})\ell(y_{n})/\sum_{n=1}^{N}w(x,y_{n}). If Z^w≜N−1​∑n=1Nw⁡(x,yn)\hat{Z}_{w}\triangleq N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{N}w(x,y_{n}) satisfies |Z^w−1|≤ϵ<1|\hat{Z}_{w}-1|\leq\epsilon<1, then

|μ^Nsn−μ|≤|μ^N−μ|+L​ϵ1−ϵ.|\hat{\mu}_{N}^{\text{sn}}-\mu|\leq\frac{|\hat{\mu}_{N}-\mu|+L\epsilon}{1-\epsilon}. (39)

Self-normalization is the empirical form used by BOLT when Z⁡(x)Z(x) is unknown. Corollary 20 shows that this operation mainly introduces prompt-level rescaling: once the empirical total weight is close to one, the normalized prompt mean is close to the oracle importance-weighted prompt mean. Proposition 21 and Corollary 22 specialize this rescaling to the Monte Carlo partition estimate Z^N​(x)\hat{Z}_{N}(x).

Proposition 21 (Standard Prompt Normalizer Concentration).

Assume r⁡(x,y)∈[rmin,rmax]r(x,y)\in[r_{\min},r_{\max}] and define Rβ≜exp⁡(rmax/β)−exp⁡(rmin/β)R_{\beta}\triangleq\exp(r_{\max}/\beta)-\exp(r_{\min}/\beta). For a fixed prompt xx, if Z^N​(x)=N−1​∑n=1Nexp⁡(r⁡(x,yn)/β)\hat{Z}_{N}(x)=N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{N}\exp(r(x,y_{n})/\beta), then

Pr⁡(|Z^N​(x)−Z⁡(x)|≥t)≤2​exp⁡(−2​N​t2Rβ2).\Pr\!\left(|\hat{Z}_{N}(x)-Z(x)|\geq t\right)\leq 2\exp\!\left(-\frac{2Nt^{2}}{R_{\beta}^{2}}\right). (40)
Corollary 22 (Uniform Prompt-Normalizer Loss Perturbation).

Under Proposition 21, for prompts x1,…,xMx_{1},\ldots,x_{M}, set si≜Z⁡(xi)/Z^N​(xi)s_{i}\triangleq Z(x_{i})/\hat{Z}_{N}(x_{i}). If 0≤ℓθ​(x,y)≤Llog0\leq\ell_{\theta}(x,y)\leq L_{\log} and w⁡(x,y)≤wmaxw(x,y)\leq w_{\max}, then with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta,

supθ|ℒ~M,N​(θ)−ℒ^M,N​(θ)|≤wmax​Llog​Rβe−rmin/β2​N​log⁡2​Mδ.\sup_{\theta}|\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)|\leq w_{\max}L_{\log}\frac{R_{\beta}e^{-r_{\min}/\beta}}{\sqrt{2N}}\sqrt{\log\frac{2M}{\delta}}. (41)

These normalizer bounds are not support guarantees. They control the loss perturbation caused by replacing Z⁡(x)Z(x) with Z^N​(x)\hat{Z}_{N}(x) on the rollouts that were actually sampled. The support barrier is a different event: whether the stored set contains the reward-bearing region that the Boltzmann target would upweight.

Proposition 23 (Reference Coverage and One-Shot Support Barrier).

Fix a prompt xx and define Aγ​(x)≜{y:r⁡(x,y)≥maxy′⁡r⁡(x,y′)−γ}A_{\gamma}(x)\triangleq\{y:r(x,y)\geq\max_{y^{\prime}}r(x,y^{\prime})-\gamma\} and pγ​(x)≜πref​(Aγ​(x)∣x)p_{\gamma}(x)\triangleq\pi_{\text{ref}}(A_{\gamma}(x)\mid x). For NN independent reference rollouts, the probability of missing Aγ​(x)A_{\gamma}(x) is (1−pγ​(x))N(1-p_{\gamma}(x))^{N}. Thus hitting Aγ​(x)A_{\gamma}(x) with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta requires

N≥log⁡(1/δ)−log⁡(1−pγ​(x))≥1−pγ​(x)pγ​(x)​log⁡1δ.N\geq\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{-\log(1-p_{\gamma}(x))}\geq\frac{1-p_{\gamma}(x)}{p_{\gamma}(x)}\log\frac{1}{\delta}. (42)

For MM prompts with pγ,min≜mini⁡pγ​(xi)>0p_{\gamma,\min}\triangleq\min_{i}p_{\gamma}(x_{i})>0, the condition N≥log⁡(M/δ)/pγ,minN\geq\log(M/\delta)/p_{\gamma,\min} suffices to hit every Aγ​(xi)A_{\gamma}(x_{i}) with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta. Moreover, any empirical target formed by nonnegative weights on the stored rollout set 𝒟x\mathcal{D}_{x} is supported on 𝒟x\mathcal{D}_{x}; if 𝒟x∩Aγ​(x)=∅\mathcal{D}_{x}\cap A_{\gamma}(x)=\emptyset, then it assigns zero mass to Aγ​(x)A_{\gamma}(x).

Corollary 24 (Rare-Support Lower Bound).

For a binary prompt with completions y+y^{+} and y−y^{-}, rewards r⁡(y+)=1r(y^{+})=1, r⁡(y−)=0r(y^{-})=0, and πref​(y+∣x)=p\pi_{\text{ref}}(y^{+}\mid x)=p, let a≜e1/βa\triangleq e^{1/\beta}, so π∗​(y+∣x)=p​a/[1+p⁡(a−1)]\pi^{*}(y^{+}\mid x)=pa/[1+p(a-1)]. With NN one-shot reference rollouts, the expected best possible support-restricted prompt gap is at least

(1−p)N​β​log⁡11−π∗​(y+∣x).(1-p)^{N}\,\beta\log\frac{1}{1-\pi^{*}(y^{+}\mid x)}. (43)

Achieving failure probability at most δ\delta for observing y+y^{+} requires N=Ω⁡(p−1​log⁡(1/δ))N=\Omega(p^{-1}\log(1/\delta)) when pp is small.

Corollary 25 (Pass@kk Support Boundary).

Let AA be the success set and let SS be the stored support. Any policy QQ supported on SS has

pass​@⁡k⁡(Q,A)=1−(1−Q⁡(A∩S))k.\operatorname{pass@}k(Q;A)=1-\left(1-Q(A\cap S)\right)^{k}. (44)

For the conditional target Q∗=P(⋅∣S)Q^{*}=P(\cdot\mid S), pass​@⁡k⁡(Q∗,A)=1−(1−P⁡(A∩S)/P⁡(S))k\operatorname{pass@}k(Q^{*};A)=1-(1-P(A\cap S)/P(S))^{k}. If A∩S=∅A\cap S=\emptyset, pass@kk is zero for every support-restricted policy and every finite kk.

Proposition 26 (Standard Optimizer-Level Normalizer Perturbation).

Let si≜Z⁡(xi)/Z^N​(xi)s_{i}\triangleq Z(x_{i})/\hat{Z}_{N}(x_{i}). Assume ‖∇ℒ~N,i​(θ)‖≤G\|\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{N,i}(\theta)\|\leq G for all i,θi,\theta, and assume ℒ~M,N\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N} satisfies the μ\mu-PL inequality. If θ^\hat{\theta} is stationary for ℒ^M,N\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}, then

ℒ~M,N​(θ^)−infθℒ~M,N​(θ)≤G22​μ​M​∑i=1M(si−1)2.\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\hat{\theta})-\inf_{\theta}\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)\leq\frac{G^{2}}{2\mu M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}(s_{i}-1)^{2}. (45)

Consequently, under the bounded-reward assumptions of Proposition 21, 𝔼[ℒ~M,N(θ^)−infθℒ~M,N(θ)]≤G2Rβ2e−2rmin/β/(8μN)\mathbb{E}[\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\hat{\theta})-\inf_{\theta}\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)]\leq G^{2}R_{\beta}^{2}e^{-2r_{\min}/\beta}/(8\mu N).

Proposition 27 (Neyman-Style Allocation Component).

For prompt xix_{i}, let Vi≜Varπref(⋅∣xi)[exp(r(xi,y)/β)]V_{i}\triangleq\operatorname{Var}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x_{i})}[\exp(r(x_{i},y)/\beta)], and let NicovN_{i}^{\text{cov}} be a required coverage count. The allocation minimizing the normalizer-variance proxy ∑iVi/Ni\sum_{i}V_{i}/N_{i} subject to Ni≥NicovN_{i}\geq N_{i}^{\text{cov}} and ∑iNi≤Btot\sum_{i}N_{i}\leq B_{\text{tot}} has the form

Ni∗=max⁡{Nicov,λ​Vi},N_{i}^{*}=\max\{N_{i}^{\text{cov}},\lambda\sqrt{V_{i}}\}, (46)

where λ\lambda is chosen so that ∑iNi∗=Btot\sum_{i}N_{i}^{*}=B_{\text{tot}} on the feasible active set.

Proposition 27 is a normalizer-variance rule after coverage floors have been chosen. It allocates extra rollouts to prompts whose partition-function estimator is noisy, but it does not replace the requirement that each prompt first receive enough samples to make useful support likely.

Proof of Theorem 6.

Fix the prompt and abbreviate P=π∗(⋅∣x)P=\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x). By the reverse-KL value identity, the distributional gap from a policy QQ is βDKL(Q∥P)\beta D_{\text{KL}}(Q\|P). If QQ is supported on SS, then

DKL(Q∥P)=∫Slogd​Qd​PdQ=∫Slogd​QdP(⋅∣S)dQ+log1P⁡(S).D_{\text{KL}}(Q\|P)=\int_{S}\log\frac{dQ}{dP}\,dQ=\int_{S}\log\frac{dQ}{dP(\cdot\mid S)}\,dQ+\log\frac{1}{P(S)}.

The first term is DKL(Q∥P(⋅∣S))≥0D_{\text{KL}}(Q\|P(\cdot\mid S))\geq 0, with equality at Q=P(⋅∣S)Q=P(\cdot\mid S). If S∩A=∅S\cap A=\emptyset, then P⁡(S)≤1−P⁡(A)P(S)\leq 1-P(A), so log⁡(1/P⁡(S))≥log⁡(1/(1−P⁡(A)))\log(1/P(S))\geq\log(1/(1-P(A))). ∎

Proof of Proposition 19.

Let Xn=w⁡(x,yn)​ℓ​(yn)X_{n}=w(x,y_{n})\ell(y_{n}). Then 𝔼⁡[Xn]=μ\mathbb{E}[X_{n}]=\mu and

Var⁡(Xn)≤𝔼⁡[Xn2]≤L2​𝔼πref​[w​(x,y)2]=L2​𝒞2​(x).\operatorname{Var}(X_{n})\leq\mathbb{E}[X_{n}^{2}]\leq L^{2}\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}}\left[w(x,y)^{2}\right]=L^{2}\mathcal{C}_{2}(x).

Also 0≤Xn≤L​wmax​(x)0\leq X_{n}\leq Lw_{\max}(x). Bernstein’s inequality gives

|μ^N−μ|≤2​L2​𝒞2​(x)​log⁡(2/δ)N+2​L​wmax​(x)​log⁡(2/δ)3​N,|\hat{\mu}_{N}-\mu|\leq\sqrt{\frac{2L^{2}\mathcal{C}_{2}(x)\log(2/\delta)}{N}}+\frac{2Lw_{\max}(x)\log(2/\delta)}{3N},

which is the displayed bound. ∎

Proof of the self-normalized part of Proposition 20.

Let Z^w≜N−1​∑n=1Nw⁡(x,yn)\hat{Z}_{w}\triangleq N^{-1}\sum_{n=1}^{N}w(x,y_{n}), so μ^Nsn=μ^N/Z^w\hat{\mu}_{N}^{\text{sn}}=\hat{\mu}_{N}/\hat{Z}_{w}. On the event |Z^w−1|≤ϵ<1|\hat{Z}_{w}-1|\leq\epsilon<1,

|μ^Nsn−μ|=|μ^N−μ+μ⁡(1−Z^w)Z^w|≤|μ^N−μ|+L​ϵ1−ϵ,|\hat{\mu}_{N}^{\text{sn}}-\mu|=\left|\frac{\hat{\mu}_{N}-\mu+\mu(1-\hat{Z}_{w})}{\hat{Z}_{w}}\right|\leq\frac{|\hat{\mu}_{N}-\mu|+L\epsilon}{1-\epsilon},

because 0≤μ≤L0\leq\mu\leq L. The normalizer event is Proposition 19 applied to the loss ℓ≡1\ell\equiv 1. ∎

Proof of Theorem 7.

The hit-probability statement is Proposition 23. The support price after a missed useful set follows from Theorem 6. The leading importance-weighted deviation is the variance term in Proposition 19. It remains to verify the binary frontier. For binary rewards, the partition function is Z=1+p⁡(a−1)Z=1+p(a-1). Therefore

π∗​(r=1∣x)=p​a/Z\pi^{*}(r=1\mid x)=pa/Z

and

𝒞2​(x)=p​(a/Z)2+(1−p)​(1/Z)2=(1−p)+p​a2[1+p⁡(a−1)]2.\mathcal{C}_{2}(x)=p(a/Z)^{2}+(1-p)(1/Z)^{2}=\frac{(1-p)+pa^{2}}{[1+p(a-1)]^{2}}.

The condition p​a/[1+p⁡(a−1)]≥1−ηpa/[1+p(a-1)]\geq 1-\eta is equivalent to

η​p​a≥(1−η)​(1−p),\eta pa\geq(1-\eta)(1-p),

which gives the lower bound on aa. Finally, since

𝒞2​(x)=π∗​(r=1∣x)2p+(1−π∗​(r=1∣x))21−p,\mathcal{C}_{2}(x)=\frac{\pi^{*}(r=1\mid x)^{2}}{p}+\frac{(1-\pi^{*}(r=1\mid x))^{2}}{1-p},

the condition π∗​(r=1∣x)≥1−η\pi^{*}(r=1\mid x)\geq 1-\eta implies 𝒞2​(x)≥(1−η)2/p\mathcal{C}_{2}(x)\geq(1-\eta)^{2}/p. ∎

Proof of the single-prompt part of Proposition 21.

The random variables exp⁡(r⁡(x,yn)/β)\exp(r(x,y_{n})/\beta) are i.i.d., have expectation Z⁡(x)Z(x), and lie in [exp⁡(rmin/β),exp⁡(rmax/β)][\exp(r_{\min}/\beta),\exp(r_{\max}/\beta)]. Hoeffding’s inequality applied to their sample mean gives the stated concentration bound [18]. ∎

For binary verifiable rewards, Z⁡(x)=1+p⁡(x)​(e1/β−1)Z(x)=1+p(x)(e^{1/\beta}-1) and Z^N​(x)=1+p^N​(x)​(e1/β−1)\hat{Z}_{N}(x)=1+\hat{p}_{N}(x)(e^{1/\beta}-1), where p⁡(x)p(x) and p^N​(x)\hat{p}_{N}(x) are the reference-policy and empirical pass rates. The Hoeffding range e1/β−1e^{1/\beta}-1 can be large when β\beta is small, but this bound alone can overstate the algorithmic damage of normalizer error. Self-normalization changes the prompt multiplier, not the positive-to-negative odds within that prompt; coverage controls whether positives appear at all.

Proof of the uniform-value part of Proposition 22.

For each prompt, define si≜Z⁡(xi)/Z^N​(xi)s_{i}\triangleq Z(x_{i})/\hat{Z}_{N}(x_{i}). Prompt-wise rescaling gives

ℒ^M,N​(θ)=1M​∑i=1Msi​ℒ~N,i​(θ),ℒ~N,i​(θ)≜1N​∑n=1Nw⁡(xi,yi,n)​ℓθ​(xi,yi,n).\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}s_{i}\,\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{N,i}(\theta),\qquad\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{N,i}(\theta)\triangleq\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N}w(x_{i},y_{i,n})\ell_{\theta}(x_{i},y_{i,n}). (47)

Since 0≤ℒ~N,i​(θ)≤wmax​Llog0\leq\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{N,i}(\theta)\leq w_{\max}L_{\log},

supθ|ℒ~M,N​(θ)−ℒ^M,N​(θ)|≤wmax​Llog​1M​∑i=1M|si−1|.\sup_{\theta}|\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)-\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)|\leq w_{\max}L_{\log}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}|s_{i}-1|. (48)

Also Z^N​(xi)≥exp⁡(rmin/β)\hat{Z}_{N}(x_{i})\geq\exp(r_{\min}/\beta), so |si−1|≤|Z⁡(xi)−Z^N​(xi)|/exp⁡(rmin/β)|s_{i}-1|\leq|Z(x_{i})-\hat{Z}_{N}(x_{i})|/\exp(r_{\min}/\beta). Applying the concentration part of Proposition 21 to all MM prompts and union bounding proves the result. ∎

Proof of Proposition 23.

For one prompt, the event of no γ\gamma-optimal rollout has probability (1−pγ​(x))N(1-p_{\gamma}(x))^{N}, proving the first claim. Accessing Aγ​(x)A_{\gamma}(x) with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta requires this failure probability to be at most δ\delta. Taking logarithms gives

N≥log⁡(1/δ)−log⁡(1−pγ​(x)).N\geq\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{-\log(1-p_{\gamma}(x))}. (49)

The inequality −log⁡(1−p)≤p/(1−p)-\log(1-p)\leq p/(1-p) for p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) gives the displayed lower bound. For MM prompts, the union bound gives

Pr⁡[∃i​ with no ​γ​-optimal rollout]≤M​(1−pγ,min)N≤M​e−N​pγ,min.\Pr[\exists i\text{ with no }\gamma\text{-optimal rollout}]\leq M(1-p_{\gamma,\min})^{N}\leq Me^{-Np_{\gamma,\min}}. (50)

Setting the right-hand side to at most δ\delta gives the sufficient condition. For the support statement, the empirical target π^v\hat{\pi}_{v} is a nonnegative measure on the atoms in 𝒟x\mathcal{D}_{x}, normalized by its total mass when that mass is positive. Hence supp⁡(π^v)⊆𝒟x\operatorname{supp}(\hat{\pi}_{v})\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{x}. If 𝒟x∩Aγ​(x)=∅\mathcal{D}_{x}\cap A_{\gamma}(x)=\emptyset, every atom assigned positive empirical mass lies outside Aγ​(x)A_{\gamma}(x), so π^v​(Aγ​(x)∣x)=0\hat{\pi}_{v}(A_{\gamma}(x)\mid x)=0 for any nonnegative weights. ∎

Proof of Corollary 24.

The Boltzmann target mass on y+y^{+} follows by substituting the two rewards into (4). With probability (1−p)N(1-p)^{N}, the stored support contains only y−y^{-}. On that event, Theorem 6 gives best possible prompt gap β​log⁡(1/(1−π∗​(y+∣x)))\beta\log(1/(1-\pi^{*}(y^{+}\mid x))). Multiplying by the event probability gives the expected lower bound. The sample-complexity statement is the condition (1−p)N≤δ(1-p)^{N}\leq\delta, equivalently N≥log⁡(1/δ)/[−log⁡(1−p)]N\geq\log(1/\delta)/[-\log(1-p)], which is Ω⁡(p−1​log⁡(1/δ))\Omega(p^{-1}\log(1/\delta)) for small pp. ∎

Proof of Corollary 25.

Since QQ is supported on SS, the event that one draw from QQ succeeds is A∩SA\cap S and has probability Q⁡(A∩S)Q(A\cap S). The probability that kk independent draws all fail is therefore (1−Q⁡(A∩S))k(1-Q(A\cap S))^{k}, giving the first display. For Q∗=P(⋅∣S)Q^{*}=P(\cdot\mid S), Q∗​(A∩S)=P⁡(A∩S)/P⁡(S)Q^{*}(A\cap S)=P(A\cap S)/P(S), which gives the second display. If S∩A=∅S\cap A=\emptyset, then Q⁡(A∩S)=0Q(A\cap S)=0 for every support-restricted QQ, so pass@kk is zero for all finite kk. ∎

Proof of Proposition 26.

By prompt-wise rescaling,

∇ℒ^M,N(θ)−∇ℒ~M,N(θ)=1M∑i=1M(si−1)∇ℒ~N,i(θ).\nabla\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)-\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}(s_{i}-1)\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{N,i}(\theta). (51)

Cauchy–Schwarz and the gradient bound imply

‖∇ℒ^M,N​(θ)−∇ℒ~M,N​(θ)‖2≤G2​1M​∑i=1M(si−1)2.\left\|\nabla\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)-\nabla\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)\right\|^{2}\leq G^{2}\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}(s_{i}-1)^{2}. (52)

At θ^\hat{\theta}, ∇ℒ^M,N​(θ^)=0\nabla\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\hat{\theta})=0. The PL inequality converts the resulting oracle gradient bound into the first displayed suboptimality bound. For the expectation, use Z^N​(xi)≥exp⁡(rmin/β)\hat{Z}_{N}(x_{i})\geq\exp(r_{\min}/\beta) and Var⁡(Z^N​(xi))≤Rβ2/(4​N)\operatorname{Var}(\hat{Z}_{N}(x_{i}))\leq R_{\beta}^{2}/(4N). ∎

For binary rewards, Vi=pi​(1−pi)​(e1/β−1)2V_{i}=p_{i}(1-p_{i})(e^{1/\beta}-1)^{2}, so the rule sends rollouts to moderately difficult prompts rather than prompts that are almost always correct or wrong. It reduces normalizer-estimation error only after reference-policy support has produced useful rollouts.

Proof of Proposition 27.

The proof of Proposition 26 with prompt-specific counts gives an upper bound proportional to ∑iVi/Ni\sum_{i}V_{i}/N_{i}. The constrained problem is convex in Ni>0N_{i}>0. The KKT conditions for inactive lower-bound constraints give −Vi/Ni2+λ=0-V_{i}/N_{i}^{2}+\lambda=0, hence Ni=λ−1/2ViN_{i}=\lambda^{-1/2}\sqrt{V_{i}}. Active constraints set Ni=NicovN_{i}=N_{i}^{\text{cov}}. Combining the two cases yields Ni∗=max⁡{Nicov,λ​Vi}N_{i}^{*}=\max\{N_{i}^{\text{cov}},\lambda\sqrt{V_{i}}\} after absorbing the inverse square root into λ\lambda, and the budget equation determines the unique λ\lambda on the feasible active set. ∎

Appendix E Generalization and Optimization Terms

Coverage is isolated in the main text because it is the one-shot error that a static objective cannot repair. Conditional on observed support, the remaining analysis is an empirical-risk chain: the population weighted likelihood is estimated by oracle reference-rollout samples, the oracle loss is perturbed by the empirical normalizer, and the optimizer returns an approximate minimizer of that empirical loss. The following statements supply the standard generalization and optimization components for that chain. Define the population target error

F(θ)≜𝔼x[DKL(π∗(⋅∣x)∥πθ(⋅∣x))],F(\theta)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[D_{\text{KL}}\!\left(\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)\,\middle\|\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)\right)\right],

and the corresponding population weighted likelihood

ℒ(θ)≜𝔼x,y∼πref[w(x,y)ℓθ(x,y)]=𝔼x𝔼y∼π∗(⋅∣x)[−logπθ(y∣x)],ℓθ≜−logπθ.\mathcal{L}(\theta)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{x,y\sim\pi_{\text{ref}}}\left[w(x,y)\ell_{\theta}(x,y)\right]=\mathbb{E}_{x}\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x)}\left[-\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x)\right],\qquad\ell_{\theta}\triangleq-\log\pi_{\theta}.

Then ℒ(θ)=F(θ)+𝔼x[H(π∗(⋅∣x))]\mathcal{L}(\theta)=F(\theta)+\mathbb{E}_{x}[H(\pi^{*}(\cdot\mid x))], so the population weighted likelihood and the forward-KL target error have the same minimizers and excess differences.

The finite algorithm replaces ℒ\mathcal{L} by empirical losses. Let ℒ~M,N\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N} use sampled prompts and reference rollouts with the true Z⁡(x)Z(x), let ℒ^M,N\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N} replace Z⁡(x)Z(x) by Z^N​(x)\hat{Z}_{N}(x), and define the empirical optimization residual

εopt≜ℒ^M,N​(θ^)−infθ∈Θℒ^M,N​(θ).\varepsilon_{\text{opt}}\triangleq\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\hat{\theta})-\inf_{\theta\in\Theta}\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta).

Theorem 9 converts this chain into a one-shot RLVR value certificate. Proposition 28 controls prompt and rollout sampling through Rademacher complexities [2]; Proposition 29 gives a posterior-predictor variant; and Propositions 30–31 separate stationarity from excess risk for stochastic optimization [13]. Appendix D supplies the normalizer perturbation. The point of the split is diagnostic: prompt sampling, rollout sampling, normalizer estimation, model class, and empirical optimization enter different residuals rather than one undifferentiated “finite sample” term.

Proposition 28 (Standard Generalization Component).

Let ℱ≜{(x,y)↦w⁡(x,y)​ℓθ​(x,y):θ∈Θ}\mathcal{F}\triangleq\{(x,y)\mapsto w(x,y)\ell_{\theta}(x,y):\theta\in\Theta\}, and assume every f∈ℱf\in\mathcal{F} takes values in [0,R][0,R]. Let ℋ≜{x↦𝔼πref(⋅∣x)[w(x,y)ℓθ(x,y)]:θ∈Θ}\mathcal{H}\triangleq\{x\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x)}[w(x,y)\ell_{\theta}(x,y)]:\theta\in\Theta\}. With probability at least 1−2​δ1-2\delta,

supθ∈Θ|ℒ⁡(θ)−ℒ~M,N​(θ)|≤\displaystyle\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}|\mathcal{L}(\theta)-\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta)|\leq 2​ℜM​(ℋ)+R​log⁡(1/δ)2​M\displaystyle 2\mathfrak{R}_{M}(\mathcal{H})+R\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2M}} (53)
+2ℜM,N(ℱ∣x1:M)+Rlog⁡(1/δ)2​M​N.\displaystyle+2\mathfrak{R}_{M,N}(\mathcal{F}\mid x_{1:M})+R\sqrt{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{2MN}}.
Proof of Proposition 28.

Use the decomposition supθ|ℒ−ℒ~M,N|≤supθ|ℒ−ℒ¯M|+supθ|ℒ¯M−ℒ~M,N|\sup_{\theta}|\mathcal{L}-\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}|\leq\sup_{\theta}|\mathcal{L}-\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{M}|+\sup_{\theta}|\bar{\mathcal{L}}_{M}-\tilde{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}|. The first term is the standard symmetrization/Rademacher complexity bound for MM prompt samples with bounded range RR [2]. Conditional on the prompts, the second term is a rollout-level empirical-process deviation for the class ℱ\mathcal{F} under the product distribution ∏i=1Mπref(⋅∣xi)N\prod_{i=1}^{M}\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x_{i})^{N}. Conditional symmetrization gives the 2ℜM,N(ℱ∣x1:M)2\mathfrak{R}_{M,N}(\mathcal{F}\mid x_{1:M}) term, and bounded differences for variables in [0,R][0,R] gives the R​log⁡(1/δ)/(M​N)R\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/(MN)} concentration term. This keeps the rollout-level function-class complexity explicit; a simpler N−1/2N^{-1/2} expression requires an additional finite-class, covering, or VC-type bound on ℜM,N(ℱ∣x1:M)\mathfrak{R}_{M,N}(\mathcal{F}\mid x_{1:M}). ∎

Proposition 29 (Weighted PAC-Bayes Certificate).

Let zj=(xj,yj)z_{j}=(x_{j},y_{j}), j=1,…,nj=1,\ldots,n, be independent samples from x∼𝒳x\sim\mathcal{X}, y∼πref(⋅∣x)y\sim\pi_{\text{ref}}(\cdot\mid x). Assume 0≤w⁡(z)​ℓθ​(z)≤R0\leq w(z)\ell_{\theta}(z)\leq R for every θ\theta and zz. Let Π\Pi be a prior over parameters independent of the samples. Then, with probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, every posterior distribution QQ over parameters satisfies

𝔼θ∼Q​ℒ​(θ)≤𝔼θ∼Q​[1n​∑j=1nw⁡(zj)​ℓθ​(zj)]+R​DKL(Q∥Π)+log((n+1)/δ)2​n.\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim Q}\mathcal{L}(\theta)\leq\mathbb{E}_{\theta\sim Q}\left[\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{n}w(z_{j})\ell_{\theta}(z_{j})\right]+R\sqrt{\frac{D_{\text{KL}}(Q\|\Pi)+\log((n+1)/\delta)}{2n}}. (54)
Proof of Proposition 29.

Apply the bounded-loss PAC-Bayes binary-kl inequality [28, 3] to the normalized loss w⁡(z)​ℓθ​(z)/R∈[0,1]w(z)\ell_{\theta}(z)/R\in[0,1]. Write L^n​(θ)≜n−1​∑j=1nw⁡(zj)​ℓθ​(zj)\hat{L}_{n}(\theta)\triangleq n^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{n}w(z_{j})\ell_{\theta}(z_{j}). With probability at least 1−δ1-\delta, all posteriors QQ satisfy

kl⁡(𝔼Q​L^n/R∥𝔼Q​ℒ/R)≤DKL(Q∥Π)+log((n+1)/δ)n.\operatorname{kl}\!\left(\mathbb{E}_{Q}\hat{L}_{n}/R\,\middle\|\,\mathbb{E}_{Q}\mathcal{L}/R\right)\leq\frac{D_{\text{KL}}(Q\|\Pi)+\log((n+1)/\delta)}{n}.

Pinsker’s inequality converts the binary-kl relation into the displayed one-sided bound. ∎

Proposition 30 (Standard SGD Stationarity Certificate).

Assume ℒ^M,N\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N} is LL-smooth and stochastic gradients gtg_{t} are unbiased with 𝔼⁡[‖gt−∇ℒ^M,N​(θt)‖2∣θt]≤σ2/B\mathbb{E}[\|g_{t}-\nabla\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t})\|^{2}\mid\theta_{t}]\leq\sigma^{2}/B. For SGD with step size η≤1/L\eta\leq 1/L, if τ\tau is uniform on {0,…,T−1}\{0,\ldots,T-1\}, then

𝔼​‖∇ℒ^M,N​(θτ)‖2≤2​(ℒ^M,N​(θ0)−infθℒ^M,N​(θ))η​T+L​η​σ2B.\mathbb{E}\|\nabla\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{\tau})\|^{2}\leq\frac{2(\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{0})-\inf_{\theta}\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta))}{\eta T}+\frac{L\eta\sigma^{2}}{B}. (55)
Corollary 31 (PL Excess-Risk Certificate).

If, in addition, ℒ^M,N\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N} satisfies the μ\mu-PL inequality and L∗≜infθℒ^M,N​(θ)L^{*}\triangleq\inf_{\theta}\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta), then

𝔼⁡[ℒ^M,N​(θT)−L∗]≤(1−η​μ)T​(ℒ^M,N​(θ0)−L∗)+L​η​σ22​μ​B.\mathbb{E}[\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{T})-L^{*}]\leq(1-\eta\mu)^{T}(\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{0})-L^{*})+\frac{L\eta\sigma^{2}}{2\mu B}. (56)
Proof of the stationarity clause in Proposition 30.

By smoothness,

ℒ^M,N​(θt+1)≤ℒ^M,N​(θt)−η⁡⟨∇ℒ^M,N​(θt),gt⟩+L​η22​‖gt‖2.\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t+1})\leq\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t})-\eta\langle\nabla\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t}),g_{t}\rangle+\frac{L\eta^{2}}{2}\left\|g_{t}\right\|^{2}. (57)

Taking conditional expectation and using unbiasedness and the variance bound gives

𝔼⁡[ℒ^M,N​(θt+1)]≤ℒ^M,N​(θt)−η2​‖∇ℒ^M,N​(θt)‖2+L​η2​σ22​B\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t+1})\right]\leq\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t})-\frac{\eta}{2}\left\|\nabla\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}+\frac{L\eta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2B} (58)

for η≤1/L\eta\leq 1/L. Summing over tt and optimizing the standard upper bound over η\eta yields (55), the usual nonconvex stochastic-gradient rate [13]. ∎

Proof of the PL clause in Proposition 31.

Let L∗≜infθℒ^M,N​(θ)L^{*}\triangleq\inf_{\theta}\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta). Smoothness, unbiasedness, and the variance bound give, for η≤1/L\eta\leq 1/L,

𝔼⁡[ℒ^M,N​(θt+1)−L∗∣θt]≤ℒ^M,N​(θt)−L∗−η2​‖∇ℒ^M,N​(θt)‖2+L​η2​σ22​B.\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t+1})-L^{*}\mid\theta_{t}\right]\leq\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t})-L^{*}-\frac{\eta}{2}\left\|\nabla\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}+\frac{L\eta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2B}.

The μ\mu-PL condition gives 12​‖∇ℒ^M,N​(θt)‖2≥μ⁡(ℒ^M,N​(θt)−L∗)\frac{1}{2}\left\|\nabla\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t})\right\|^{2}\geq\mu(\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t})-L^{*}). Therefore

𝔼⁡[ℒ^M,N​(θt+1)−L∗]≤(1−η​μ)​𝔼​[ℒ^M,N​(θt)−L∗]+L​η2​σ22​B.\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t+1})-L^{*}\right]\leq(1-\eta\mu)\mathbb{E}\left[\hat{\mathcal{L}}_{M,N}(\theta_{t})-L^{*}\right]+\frac{L\eta^{2}\sigma^{2}}{2B}.

Unrolling the recursion and using ∑j=0T−1(1−η​μ)j≤1/(η​μ)\sum_{j=0}^{T-1}(1-\eta\mu)^{j}\leq 1/(\eta\mu) gives (56). ∎

Proposition 30 and Corollary 31 record the two optimization certificates. The stationarity result controls average stationarity of the empirical objective, not value optimality by itself. The PL result is the certificate that can be inserted directly into the residual εopt\varepsilon_{\text{opt}} used in Theorem 9. Keeping the two statements distinct prevents a nonconvex stationarity certificate from being silently treated as an excess-risk certificate, and it keeps optimization error distinct from the statistical errors caused by finite reference rollouts.

Apply Proposition 28 to Δgen\Delta_{\text{gen}}, Proposition 21 to Δnorm\Delta_{\text{norm}}, and Proposition 31 to εopt\varepsilon_{\text{opt}} when the PL condition is assumed. Substitute these bounds into Theorem 9 and absorb universal constants into ≲\lesssim. ∎

Proof of Theorem 9.

By (30),

𝒥RL(π∗)−𝒥RL(πθ^)=β𝔼x[DKL(πθ^∥π∗)].\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi^{*})-\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi_{\hat{\theta}})=\beta\mathbb{E}_{x}\left[D_{\text{KL}}(\pi_{\hat{\theta}}\|\pi^{*})\right]. (60)

On ℰτ\mathcal{E}_{\tau}, Theorem 6 gives, for each prompt, support-restricted gap at most β​log⁡(1/(1−τi))\beta\log(1/(1-\tau_{i})). Appendix F KL-PMD Proofs for Iterative BOLT

Iterative BOLT reuses the same Boltzmann projection after refreshing the reference policy. Exact rounds accumulate reward tilts in closed form, while inexact rounds are controlled by the relative-entropy mirror-descent potential. The proof sequence therefore separates the ideal distribution-space trajectory from the practical inner-solver error that appears when each weighted-SFT round only approximates the exact mirror step. This is the iterative analogue of the one-shot separation between the target projection and finite optimization error.

Exact-path consequences.

The exact KL-PMD path supplies the coverage interpretations used in the main text. They are special cases of the same Boltzmann tilt accumulated across refreshed rounds. In the binary verifier specialization, with p0≜πθ0​(r=1∣x)∈(0,1)p_{0}\triangleq\pi_{\theta_{0}}(r=1\mid x)\in(0,1) and r∈{0,1}r\in\{0,1\},

pk≜πθk​(r=1∣x)=p0​ek/β1+p0​(ek/β−1).p_{k}\triangleq\pi_{\theta_{k}}(r=1\mid x)=\frac{p_{0}e^{k/\beta}}{1+p_{0}(e^{k/\beta}-1)}. (63)

With NN rollouts in each of KK refreshed rounds,

Prefresh=1−∏k=0K−1(1−pk)N,Pone=1−(1−p0)K​N,P_{\text{refresh}}=1-\prod_{k=0}^{K-1}(1-p_{k})^{N},\qquad P_{\text{one}}=1-(1-p_{0})^{KN},

and Prefresh>PoneP_{\text{refresh}}>P_{\text{one}} for K>1K>1.

Under Theorem 11, let 𝒴∗​(x)≜arg​maxy⁡r​(x,y)\mathcal{Y}^{*}(x)\triangleq\argmax_{y}r(x,y) and p∗​(x)≜πθ0​(𝒴∗​(x)∣x)>0p_{*}(x)\triangleq\pi_{\theta_{0}}(\mathcal{Y}^{*}(x)\mid x)>0. If the strict reward gap γ⁡(x)≜r∗​(x)−maxy∉𝒴∗​(x)⁡r⁡(x,y)>0\gamma(x)\triangleq r^{*}(x)-\max_{y\notin\mathcal{Y}^{*}(x)}r(x,y)>0 exists, then

1−πθK​(𝒴∗​(x)∣x)\displaystyle 1-\pi_{\theta_{K}}(\mathcal{Y}^{*}(x)\mid x) ≤1−p∗​(x)p∗​(x)e−Kγ(x)/β,\displaystyle\leq\frac{1-p_{*}(x)}{p_{*}(x)}e^{-K\gamma(x)/\beta}, (64)
r∗​(x)−𝔼πθK​[r⁡(x,y)]\displaystyle r^{*}(x)-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\theta_{K}}}[r(x,y)] ≤Δr1−p∗​(x)p∗​(x)e−Kγ(x)/β.\displaystyle\leq\Delta r\frac{1-p_{*}(x)}{p_{*}(x)}e^{-K\gamma(x)/\beta}.

Finally, for a desired effective temperature βeff>0\beta_{\text{eff}}>0, set a⋆≜1/βeffa_{\star}\triangleq 1/\beta_{\text{eff}}. Exact iteration with per-round temperature β\beta realizes the lattice aK≜K/βa_{K}\triangleq K/\beta. Choosing KK nearest to β​a⋆\beta a_{\star} gives |aK−a⋆|≤1/(2​β)|a_{K}-a_{\star}|\leq 1/(2\beta), and if πa⋆\pi_{a_{\star}} is the ideal Boltzmann policy at the target effective temperature, then

supy|log⁡πaK​(y)πa⋆​(y)|≤Δ​r2​β,TV⁡(πaK,πa⋆)≤tanh⁡(Δ​r4​β).\sup_{y}\left|\log\frac{\pi_{a_{K}}(y)}{\pi_{a_{\star}}(y)}\right|\leq\frac{\Delta r}{2\beta},\qquad\operatorname{TV}(\pi_{a_{K}},\pi_{a_{\star}})\leq\tanh\!\left(\frac{\Delta r}{4\beta}\right).

For a binary reference pass probability p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1), exact iteration with β≥βeff\beta\geq\beta_{\text{eff}} and K⁡(β)≜⌈β/βeff⌉K(\beta)\triangleq\lceil\beta/\beta_{\text{eff}}\rceil has ESS-driven sampling cost proxy

CESS​(β,p,βeff)≜K⁡(β)​(1−p)+p​e2/β[1+p⁡(e1/β−1)]2.C_{\text{ESS}}(\beta;p,\beta_{\text{eff}})\triangleq K(\beta)\,\frac{(1-p)+pe^{2/\beta}}{[1+p(e^{1/\beta}-1)]^{2}}. (65)
Corollary 33 (Reward-Gap Hit-Rate Bound).

Under the assumptions of Corollary 12, let p¯k(x)≜[1+{(1−p0(x))/p0(x)}exp(−kγ(x)/β)]−1\underline{p}_{k}(x)\triangleq[1+\{(1-p_{0}(x))/p_{0}(x)\}\exp(-k\gamma(x)/\beta)]^{-1}. Then pk​(x)≥p¯k​(x)p_{k}(x)\geq\underline{p}_{k}(x) and

Thus a total refreshed budget K​NKN reaches hit probability 1−δ1-\delta once K​N≳log⁡(1/δ)/(K−1​∑kp¯k​(x))KN\gtrsim\log(1/\delta)/(K^{-1}\sum_{k}\underline{p}_{k}(x)), whereas fixed one-shot sampling costs order p0​(x)−1​log⁡(1/δ)p_{0}(x)^{-1}\log(1/\delta).

For a fixed prompt, the KKT condition for minimizing −⟨r,π⟩+βDKL(π∥qk)-\langle r,\pi\rangle+\beta D_{\text{KL}}(\pi\|q_{k}) under ∑yπ⁡(y)=1\sum_{y}\pi(y)=1 is

−r⁡(y)+β⁡(log⁡π⁡(y)−log⁡qk​(y)+1)+λ=0.-r(y)+\beta\left(\log\pi(y)-\log q_{k}(y)+1\right)+\lambda=0. (71)

Proof of Proposition 34.

Fix a prompt and set qk=πθk(⋅∣x)q_{k}=\pi_{\theta_{k}}(\cdot\mid x) throughout; averaging the promptwise inequality over xx gives the corresponding population statement. For the exact mirror step qk+1ex​(y)∝qk​(y)​exp⁡(r⁡(y)/β)q_{k+1}^{\text{ex}}(y)\propto q_{k}(y)\exp(r(y)/\beta),

Quadratic growth gives ‖θk+1−θ^k∗‖≤2​ξk/μk\|\theta_{k+1}-\hat{\theta}_{k}^{*}\|\leq\sqrt{2\xi_{k}/\mu_{k}}. Proof of Proposition 13.

Apply the prompt-wise Proposition 34 and then average over prompts. The certified drift condition (25) supplies the prompt-averaged inexact error term εk†\varepsilon_{k}^{\dagger} at each round. Substituting these drift terms into the inexact mirror-descent regret bound gives (26). ∎

Proof of Corollary 36.

For each round kk, condition on the history 𝒢k\mathcal{G}_{k}. The data drawn in that round are fresh under the current sampler, so the stated conditional generalization and normalizer bounds hold with conditional failure probability at most δgen,k+δnorm,k\delta_{\text{gen},k}+\delta_{\text{norm},k}. Applying a union bound over rounds gives simultaneous success with probability at least 1−∑k(δgen,k+δnorm,k)1-\sum_{k}(\delta_{\text{gen},k}+\delta_{\text{norm},k}). On this simultaneous event, substitute the deterministic bounds Gk​(δgen,k)G_{k}(\delta_{\text{gen},k}) and Nk​(δnorm,k)N_{k}(\delta_{\text{norm},k}) for Δgen,k\Delta_{\text{gen},k} and Δnorm,k\Delta_{\text{norm},k} in Corollary 14, or use the certified drift terms directly in Proposition 13. ∎

The temperature-cost remark in the main text follows from these exact-path identities. A one-shot run chooses its final temperature directly: too small a β\beta gives sharp but high-variance weights, while too large a β\beta barely moves the policy. Exact iterative BOLT separates the per-round stability decision from the final effective temperature. A conservative per-round temperature keeps each weighted-SFT problem stable, and additional rounds traverse lower effective temperatures. The discrete-lattice bound quantifies how closely a chosen number of rounds approximates a desired effective temperature, while the ESS rule ties that stable per-round choice to the reference pass probability and weight variance.

Appendix G Additional Robustness and Implementation Consequences

The theory trunk centers on target identification, finite one-shot replacement, and refreshed KL-PMD. Several implementation choices still act through the same induced-target view. Clipping changes the target rather than merely stabilizing optimization, bounded verifier error perturbs the Boltzmann policy before training begins, and token-level coefficients reproduce a sequence-level target only when they equal the appropriate marginal density ratios.

Clipping stabilizes large density-ratio weights, but it changes the policy being fitted unless the cap is inactive. The best clipped objective is therefore not an unbiased version of BOLT; it is the closest capped induced target in reverse KL to the desired Boltzmann target.

Proposition 37 (Capped Density-Ratio Projection).

Fix a prompt and sampler qq, and let P≪qP\ll q have density w⋆​(y)≜d​P/d​q​(y)>0w^{\star}(y)\triangleq dP/dq(y)>0 qq-almost surely. For a cap c≥1c\geq 1, consider normalized capped weights 𝒰c≜{u: 0≤u(y)≤c,𝔼q[u]=1}\mathcal{U}_{c}\triangleq\{u:\;0\leq u(y)\leq c,\ \mathbb{E}_{q}[u]=1\}, with Qu​(d​y)≜u⁡(y)​q​(d​y)Q_{u}(dy)\triangleq u(y)q(dy). The minimizer of DKL(Qu∥P)D_{\text{KL}}(Q_{u}\|P) over u∈𝒰cu\in\mathcal{U}_{c} is

uc(y)=min{αw⋆(y),c},𝔼q[uc]=1,infu∈𝒰cDKL(Qu∥P)=DKL(Quc∥P),u_{c}(y)=\min\{\alpha w^{\star}(y),c\},\qquad\mathbb{E}_{q}[u_{c}]=1,\qquad\inf_{u\in\mathcal{U}_{c}}D_{\text{KL}}(Q_{u}\|P)=D_{\text{KL}}(Q_{u_{c}}\|P), (74)

where α>0\alpha>0 is chosen uniquely by the normalization equation. For P=π∗P=\pi^{*} and q=πrefq=\pi_{\text{ref}}, the best fixed-reference RLVR gap achievable by normalized capped reference-sampled weights is βDKL(Quc∥π∗)\beta\,D_{\text{KL}}(Q_{u_{c}}\|\pi^{*}).

Proof.

The feasible set is convex and nonempty because c≥1c\geq 1 and u≡1u\equiv 1 is feasible. The objective is

DKL(Qu∥P)=∫u(y)logu⁡(y)w⋆​(y)dq(y),D_{\text{KL}}(Q_{u}\|P)=\int u(y)\log\frac{u(y)}{w^{\star}(y)}\,dq(y),

which is strictly convex in uu on the support where u>0u>0. The KKT conditions for the constraint 𝔼q​[u]=1\mathbb{E}_{q}[u]=1 and the upper bound u≤cu\leq c give, on the non-capped region,

log⁡u⁡(y)w⋆​(y)+1+λ=0,\log\frac{u(y)}{w^{\star}(y)}+1+\lambda=0,

so u⁡(y)=α​w⋆​(y)u(y)=\alpha w^{\star}(y) for α=e−1−λ\alpha=e^{-1-\lambda}. On the capped region, complementary slackness gives u⁡(y)=cu(y)=c. Hence every minimizer has the form uc​(y)=min⁡{α​w⋆​(y),c}u_{c}(y)=\min\{\alpha w^{\star}(y),c\}. The map α↦𝔼q​[min⁡{α​w⋆,c}]\alpha\mapsto\mathbb{E}_{q}[\min\{\alpha w^{\star},c\}] is continuous and strictly increasing from 00 to cc, so for c≥1c\geq 1 there is a unique α\alpha with expectation 11. The RLVR gap statement follows from (30). ∎

Verifier perturbations act at the same target level. If the reward used for weighting differs from the intended verifier reward, the induced Boltzmann target changes before any optimizer or finite-sample effect appears. Proposition 38 gives the resulting target-stability bound for uniformly bounded reward error.

Proposition 38 (Bounded Verifier-Perturbation Stability).

Fix a prompt and let π∗\pi^{*} be the Boltzmann target for reward rr. Let π~∗\tilde{\pi}^{*} be the Boltzmann target obtained from an imperfect reward r~\tilde{r} with supy|r~​(y)−r⁡(y)|≤ϵ\sup_{y}|\tilde{r}(y)-r(y)|\leq\epsilon. Then

supy|log⁡π~∗​(y)π∗​(y)|\displaystyle\sup_{y}\left|\log\frac{\tilde{\pi}^{*}(y)}{\pi^{*}(y)}\right| ≤2​ϵβ,\displaystyle\leq\frac{2\epsilon}{\beta}, TV⁡(π~∗,π∗)\displaystyle\operatorname{TV}(\tilde{\pi}^{*},\pi^{*}) ≤tanh⁡(ϵβ).\displaystyle\leq\tanh\!\left(\frac{\epsilon}{\beta}\right). (75)
𝒥RL​(π∗)−𝒥RL​(π~∗)\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\pi^{*})-\mathcal{J}_{\text{RL}}(\tilde{\pi}^{*}) =βDKL(π~∗∥π∗)≤2ϵ.\displaystyle=\beta D_{\text{KL}}(\tilde{\pi}^{*}\|\pi^{*})\leq 2\epsilon.
Proof.

Write Δ​(y)=r~​(y)−r​(y)\Delta(y)=\tilde{r}(y)-r(y) and let Z~\tilde{Z} and ZZ be the corresponding prompt partition functions. Since |Δ⁡(y)|≤ϵ|\Delta(y)|\leq\epsilon,

e−ϵ/βZ≤Z~≤eϵ/βZ.e^{-\epsilon/\beta}Z\leq\tilde{Z}\leq e^{\epsilon/\beta}Z.

Therefore

log⁡π~∗​(y)π∗​(y)=Δ⁡(y)β−log⁡Z~Z,\log\frac{\tilde{\pi}^{*}(y)}{\pi^{*}(y)}=\frac{\Delta(y)}{\beta}-\log\frac{\tilde{Z}}{Z},

whose absolute value is at most 2​ϵ/β2\epsilon/\beta. If two distributions have likelihood ratio in [e−a,ea][e^{-a},e^{a}], then their total variation distance is at most tanh⁡(a/2)\tanh(a/2); here a=2​ϵ/βa=2\epsilon/\beta. The KL bound follows from DKL(π~∗∥π∗)=𝔼π~∗[log(π~∗/π∗)]≤2ϵ/βD_{\text{KL}}(\tilde{\pi}^{*}\|\pi^{*})=\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{\pi}^{*}}[\log(\tilde{\pi}^{*}/\pi^{*})]\leq 2\epsilon/\beta, and the RLVR value identity gives the final display. ∎

Sequence-level weighting and token-level weighting are also different target statements. A single sequence weight multiplies every token log probability in that completion, whereas token-level coefficients define local conditional targets at each prefix. They are equivalent only when the token coefficients are the marginal density ratios induced by the desired sequence-level target.

Proposition 39 (Token-Level Coefficients Needed for a Sequence Target).

Fix a prompt and a finite completion length TT. Let q(y1:T)q(y_{1:T}) be a rollout distribution and let P(y1:T)=q(y1:T)w(y1:T)P(y_{1:T})=q(y_{1:T})w(y_{1:T}) with 𝔼q​[w]=1\mathbb{E}_{q}[w]=1. The sequence-level weighted loss 𝔼q[w(Y1:T)∑t=1T−logπθ(Yt∣Y<t)]\mathbb{E}_{q}[w(Y_{1:T})\sum_{t=1}^{T}-\log\pi_{\theta}(Y_{t}\mid Y_{<t})] is exactly equal, as a functional of the token log-probabilities, to the token-weighted loss ∑t=1T𝔼q​[vt​(Y<t,Yt)​{−log⁡πθ​(Yt∣Y<t)}]\sum_{t=1}^{T}\mathbb{E}_{q}[v_{t}(Y_{<t},Y_{t})\{-\log\pi_{\theta}(Y_{t}\mid Y_{<t})\}] if and only if, for every prefix-token pair with positive qq-mass,

vt(h,a)=P⁡(Y<t=h,Yt=a)q⁡(Y<t=h,Yt=a)=𝔼q[w(Y1:T)∣Y<t=h,Yt=a].v_{t}(h,a)=\frac{P(Y_{<t}=h,Y_{t}=a)}{q(Y_{<t}=h,Y_{t}=a)}=\mathbb{E}_{q}\!\left[w(Y_{1:T})\mid Y_{<t}=h,Y_{t}=a\right]. (76)

Consequently, generic tokenwise weights induce local token targets proportional to q⁡(Yt=a∣h)​vt​(h,a)q(Y_{t}=a\mid h)v_{t}(h,a), which need not equal the sequence-target conditional P⁡(Yt=a∣h)P(Y_{t}=a\mid h).

Proof.

Expand the sequence-level loss by collecting the coefficient of each −log⁡πθ​(a∣h)-\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid h) term:

∑t,h,aP⁡(Y<t=h,Yt=a)​{−log⁡πθ​(a∣h)}.\sum_{t,h,a}P(Y_{<t}=h,Y_{t}=a)\{-\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid h)\}.

The token-weighted loss has the corresponding expansion

∑t,h,aq⁡(Y<t=h,Yt=a)​vt​(h,a)​{−log⁡πθ​(a∣h)}.\sum_{t,h,a}q(Y_{<t}=h,Y_{t}=a)v_{t}(h,a)\{-\log\pi_{\theta}(a\mid h)\}.

The two objectives are equal for all θ\theta if and only if the coefficients of every token log-probability agree, which gives the displayed condition. Normalizing the coefficients for a fixed prefix hh shows that a generic token-weighted objective fits the local conditional target proportional to q⁡(Yt=a∣h)​vt​(h,a)q(Y_{t}=a\mid h)v_{t}(h,a). ∎

Appendix H Experiment Protocol, Checkpoint Curves, and Auxiliary Checks

The appendix evidence supports the two empirical claims made in the main text: target-matched weighting changes the fitted policy under a fixed sampler, and sampler refresh can move beyond a saturated one-shot objective. It therefore reports the full checkpoint grids behind Tables 2 and 3, plus a retention check after GSM8K fine-tuning. SFT trains on ground-truth demonstrations, VAR is treated as a demonstration-based weighted SFT method, GRPO is the online rollout baseline, and Refit uses reference-policy rollouts with raw rewards as weights. BOLT uses the same type of reference rollouts as Refit but weights them by the empirical prompt-normalized Boltzmann weight exp⁡(r/β)/Z^N​(x)\exp(r/\beta)/\hat{Z}_{N}(x), so the Refit–BOLT contrast holds the sampler fixed while changing the induced target. The resource and retention measurements use Qwen3-8B [48] with LoRA fine-tuning [20]. The checkpoint curves add Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3.5-9B runs; within each sweep, methods are compared on the same recorded checkpoint grid unless an entry is missing in the source results.

H.1 Full Checkpoint Curves

The full checkpoint curves make the learning dynamics visible rather than only the selected best checkpoints. They show whether a method improves through an early peak, saturates on fixed reference rollouts, or continues to improve after sampler refresh. Empty source tables for unreported code benchmarks are not reproduced, because they would add table mass without empirical measurements.

H.2 Retention Check

The retention evaluation asks a narrower question than the main projection tables. After GSM8K fine-tuning, it evaluates PIQA, HellaSwag, Winogrande, and RACE-high to check whether methods trained on reference-policy rollouts stay closer to the base distribution than demonstration-only baselines in the reported setup. The table is not a complete forgetting benchmark: it uses single-run values from the reported runs, and multi-seed variation, confidence intervals, and exact hardware descriptions are not yet included.

SFT and VAR improve RACE-high but lose more on PIQA and Winogrande, suggesting task transfer mixed with distributional overfit. Rollout-based methods stay closer to the base model, consistent with a data source anchored to the reference policy. In this setup, BOLT has the smallest drops on PIQA and Winogrande and remains near the base model on HellaSwag and RACE-high. This supports the narrow retention conclusion that reference rollouts can help anchor the fine-tuning distribution. Retention remains an empirical property to measure directly rather than a consequence inferred from the projection theory.
